title: Psalm 68: God Arises and Marches in Triumph
summary: God rises, and his enemies scatter. The psalm celebrates him as father of the fatherless and defender of widows, recalls his march from Sinai through the wilderness and his victories over kings, and describes his choice of Zion over the proud mountains of Bashan. It ends with a festive procession into the sanctuary and a call to all the kingdoms of the earth to sing to the God who rides the ancient heavens.
story: Psalm 68 is the climax of the praise psalms in 65 to 68 and one of the grandest poems in the Psalter. It tells Israel's story as a single triumphal march: from Sinai, through the wilderness, into the land, and up to God's dwelling on Zion. Where Psalm 67 prayed that the nations would praise God, Psalm 68 pictures kings bringing gifts and distant nations stretching out their hands to him. It stands just before a return to lament in Psalms 69 to 71, and it gives Book II one of its fullest pictures of God as the warrior king who rescues the weak and establishes his dwelling among his people.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David. Many interpreters connect it with David's bringing of the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6), a procession with music and dancing, because the psalm describes God's procession into the sanctuary (verses 24 and 25). Verse 1 echoes the words Moses spoke whenever the ark set out in the wilderness (Numbers 10:35), and verses 7 and 8 closely parallel Deborah's song in Judges 5:4-5, which describes the earth shaking and the heavens pouring rain when God marched from Seir. The reference to the temple at Jerusalem (verse 29) has led some scholars to date the psalm after Solomon built the temple, while others note that the word temple was also used for the tabernacle.

Psalm 68 is widely regarded as one of the most difficult texts in the Hebrew Bible. It contains rare words, abrupt shifts, and lines whose meaning is uncertain. Some scholars have suggested it is a collection of fragments or the opening lines of older songs strung together; others see a unified liturgy for a festival procession. The tribes named in verse 27, Benjamin and Judah from the south and Zebulun and Naphtali from the north, suggest a gathering of all Israel, which fits the united kingdom of David and Solomon but could reflect other settings.
cultural:
Verse 4 calls God the one who rides on the clouds, and verse 33 speaks of him riding upon the highest heavens. Texts from Ugarit, an ancient city on the Syrian coast, give the Canaanite storm god Baal the title rider of the clouds. The psalm claims that title for Israel's God: it is not Baal but the LORD who rides the storm, sends rain, and rules the heavens. The Hebrew of verse 4 is disputed; it can also be read as rides through the deserts, and translations differ.

Mount Bashan (verses 15 and 16) refers to the high country east of the Sea of Galilee, possibly including Mount Hermon, a massive peak far taller than Zion. The psalm pictures these great mountains looking with envy at the small hill God chose for his dwelling. Zalmon (verse 14) is a mountain near Shechem (Judges 9:48), and the image of snow falling on it may picture scattered, fleeing kings or the gleam of discarded weapons. In the procession, singers lead, musicians follow, and young women play tambourines, as Miriam and the women did after the crossing of the sea (Exodus 15:20). The beast in the reeds (verse 30) probably symbolizes Egypt, the land of the Nile's reeds, and Cush was the kingdom south of Egypt in what is now Sudan.
literary: The psalm is built as a procession with several movements. Verses 1 to 6 announce God's rising and describe him as defender of the weak. Verses 7 to 10 recall the march from Sinai and the gift of rain in the land. Verses 11 to 14 describe victory over kings, announced by women heralds. Verses 15 to 18 celebrate God's choice of Zion. Verses 19 to 23 praise God as deliverer from death and judge of enemies. Verses 24 to 27 describe the procession into the sanctuary. Verses 28 to 35 call on God to show his strength and invite the kingdoms of the earth to sing. The poem uses many names for God, including Elohim, the LORD, Yah (a short form of the divine name), Adonai, Shaddai (the Almighty), and the God of Israel. Images of movement, rising, marching, riding, ascending, and processing drive the whole psalm forward.

outline.t: God arises, his enemies scatter, the righteous rejoice
Father of the fatherless and defender of widows
The march from Sinai and the rain on God's inheritance
Kings flee, and the women proclaim the victory
God chooses Zion and ascends on high
The God who bears our burden and rescues from death
Kings bring gifts, Egypt and Cush reach out to God
All kingdoms sing to the rider of the heavens

doctrines.note: The psalm pictures God as the victorious king who marches from Sinai to Zion, defeats his enemies, and receives tribute from the nations. His kingdom is universal, and its capital is the place he chose to dwell among his people.

The mighty God who rides the heavens is also a father of the fatherless and defender of widows, who settles the lonely in families. The psalm refuses to separate God's power from his care for the weak.
God daily bears his people's burden and is their rescuer from death. Salvation in this psalm includes protection, provision, deliverance from enemies, and escape from death itself.
The psalm ends with Egypt and Cush reaching out to God and the kingdoms of the earth summoned to sing to him. The God of Israel is the God of all nations.

words.note: Av, father. Verse 5 calls God a father of the fatherless. In ancient Israel orphans and widows were the most vulnerable members of society, without a male protector to defend them in court or provide land. God takes that role himself, and the law commanded Israel to care for them in his name (Exodus 22:22-24; Deuteronomy 10:18).

Basar, to bear good tidings. In verse 11 a great company of women proclaim the news of victory; the Hebrew uses a feminine form. It was customary for women to celebrate victories with song (1 Samuel 18:6-7). The same verb is used in Isaiah 40:9 and 52:7 for the herald of good news, and its Greek equivalent gives the New Testament its word for proclaiming the gospel.

Mattanah, gift. Verse 18 says God has received gifts from men, even from the rebellious. Victorious kings received tribute from the conquered. Paul quotes this verse in Ephesians 4:8 with the wording that he gave gifts to men, a difference discussed under the hard question below.

Rakhav, to ride. God rides on the clouds or through the deserts (verse 4) and upon the highest heavens (verse 33). The image is of a divine warrior riding in his chariot, and the chariots of God in verse 17 are countless. It asserts that Israel's God, not Baal, rules the storm and the sky.

christ: Paul quotes verse 18 in Ephesians 4:8-10, applying it to Christ's ascension: the one who descended is the one who ascended far above all the heavens, and he gives gifts to his church, apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers. The psalm's picture of God ascending in triumph with captives in his train becomes Paul's picture of the risen Christ, victorious over sin, death, and hostile powers (Colossians 2:15). The rider of the heavens is the one who, in the Gospels, will come on the clouds (Mark 14:62). The father of the fatherless is revealed in Christ, who promised not to leave his disciples as orphans (John 14:18). And the nations reaching out to God find their answer in the gospel going to Ethiopia (Acts 8:26-39), the region the psalm calls Cush, and to the ends of the earth.

hard.q: Why does Paul quote verse 18 as saying Christ gave gifts, when the psalm says God received gifts?
hard.a: The Hebrew of verse 18 says God has “received gifts from men,” but Paul in Ephesians 4:8 says he gave gifts to men. Several explanations are offered. Some scholars note that ancient Jewish interpretation, including the Aramaic paraphrase of the Psalms known as the Targum, also read the verse as giving, so Paul may be following an existing interpretive tradition. Others point out that a conqueror who received tribute then distributed spoils to his followers, so receiving and giving are two sides of the same victory. Others suggest Paul is interpreting the psalm in light of Christ, who received the Spirit from the Father and poured him out on his people (Acts 2:33). Most agree that Paul is not misquoting carelessly but reading the psalm as fulfilled in the ascension.

questions: God is described as a father of the fatherless and defender of widows. Who are the vulnerable people around you, and how might you reflect God's care for them?
Verse 19 says the Lord daily bears our burden. What burden do you need to hand over to him today?
The psalm pictures all nations coming to worship God. How does this vision of the future shape the way you live now?
